#837. Germany slips in climate protection rankings as other countries make gains

Record renewable energy growth is driving climate progress in some countries, but Germany and many major emitters are falling behind.

Germany has slipped down the climate action ranking for the third consecutive year, with the former green leader now being outperformed by Brazil, Colombia and Romania.

In its worst performance since 2019, the country fell to place 25 and received a "medium" rating overall on the yearly Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI), which assesses efforts to curb global warming in 64 countries plus the European Union.

Still, "a number of countries have been making good progress for years," said Jan Burck, CCPI lead author, in a statement. Denmark is leading the way across all four categories assessed — energy use, greenhouse gas emissions, renewable energy and national climate policy. A total of 15 states, including Lithuania, Chile, and Morocco, received an overall "high" rating, which is two more than last year.

The European Union also moved up a spot, while Hungary jumped 21 places after the ousting of former prime minister Viktor Orban's government, which had repeatedly vetoed EU climate plans, dismissing them as a "utopian fantasy."

The top three positions on the CCPI remained vacant again this year, as no country has yet done enough to meet global climate goals aimed at preventing worsening weather extremes and climate damage.

"We are seeing a striking contrast," said Burck. "Progress on climate action is often slow and in some countries, such as the United States, things are even moving backwards. But technologically and economically there is enormous momentum."

That momentum is apparent in record solar energy growth. Last year 75% of global electricity demand growth was met by the green energy source, according to energy think tank Ember's latest global electricity review. Investment in clean energy has also outpaced that in fossil fuels for multiple years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The rapid expansion of renewable technology, as well as the Iran War and a reduction in deforestation are behind a projected slight fall in emissions for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the CCPI.

"Governments have to act now to turn the momentum into sustained emissions reductions," said CCPI co-author Niklas Höhne of the NewClimate Institute, which compiles the report with environmental NGO Germanwatch.

Burck attributed Germany's worst ever performance in the category of national climate policy to current policies being pursued by Germany's economy minister Katherina Reiche.

"Measures that primarily aim to increase the use of natural gas, threaten to undermine progress in the energy transition and risk significantly worsening the conditions for renewable energy and electrification for many years to come," said Burck.

A European Commission report published on November 9 on the sidelines of the UN COP31 climate summit in Turkey said Germany was one of nine EU countries set to miss 2030 emissions reductions targets.

Germany is not alone in its disappointing ranking. The other G20 countries — the world's leading industrialized and emerging economies, responsible for around 80% of global CO2 emissions — also perform poorly.

The only exception among them is the United Kingdom, which ranks seventh and received a high rating, performing well in greenhouse gas emissions, energy use and climate policy. However, study authors rated it low for renewable energy expansion.

The G20's oil- and gas-producing countries occupy some of the lowest positions on the climate action table. The United States, which is the world's second largest emitter, languishes alongside Russia, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Canada around the bottom of the league, with an overall rating of "very low."

The hosts of this year's COP31, also received a "low" overall score. Australia, a major coal exporter with some of the world's highest per-capita emissions, ranks 54th, while Turkey, which is also heavily dependent on fossil fuels, comes in 53rd.

China is the world's largest emitter of greenhouse gases and ranks 56th in the CCPI, receiving an overall rating of "very low." Its main weaknesses include its now high per-capita emissions and substantial energy consumption.

However, among the G20, China leads the way in renewable energy expansion. The country, which is five years ahead of schedule in reaching its goal of adding 1,200 GW of wind and solar capacity to the grid by 2030, also produces over 80% of the world's solar panels.

Several oil-producing countries, including Kazakhstan, Saudi Arabia, Uzbekistan and the United Arab Emirates, are also performing better than expected in the renewables category and "are significantly expanding their previously limited" capacity, said the report.

The authors said these countries have significant potential to further expand renewables.

"In the Arab states in particular, very high per-capita emissions and an above-average level of electrification coincide with a relatively low existing share of renewable energy and enormous solar potential," said co-author Natalie Pelekh in a statement. "These are, in fact, ideal conditions for more ambitious climate action."

This article was originally published in German.

#836. From Dunfermline to Dubai - McPake on new life in Middle East

James McPake may not have given up on football management but the former Dundee and Dunfermline Athletic boss is discovering there is life beyond the dugout.

Four months after moving to Dubai with his family, the 41-year-old has settled into a new role working in schools to develop young players.

It is a considerable change from the pressures of Scottish football but one that McPake and his family had been contemplating for more than a year.

His wife Dawn, a teacher, secured a position in Dubai before McPake landed his own opportunity, one that has opened up a different world of opportunities, including working alongside some recognisable names in football.

"It's certainly a bit different from back home but we're enjoying it," said McPake, who won an international cap with Northern Ireland in 2012.

"There is obviously a big demand for British curriculum teachers, so Dawn managed to get a position and I've been pretty fortunate to land here."

The timing of the family's move has inevitably attracted attention, given the wider tensions in the Middle East and concerns about security in the region.

However, McPake insists their experience of living in Dubai has been very different from some of the headlines.

"You don't hear a lot about it and you don't see anything. It is very much business as usual," he explains. "It's as busy as when we've come here on holiday. It's just like being anywhere else.

"The girls are enjoying it. They feel safe, they enjoy school and they can go out and play at night. We've had no issues that I've seen."

McPake's decision to head overseas has also provided an opportunity to step away from the demands of management and concentrate on developing players.

His responsibilities include overseeing under-16 and under-19 programmes at an impressive set-up, with school timetables adapted to accommodate training and facilities including strength and conditioning rooms, pools and pitches.

"The programme is relatively new but it's similar to the way you would look at an SFA performance school," he says. "The facilities are fantastic. It's difficult not to make a difference when you have facilities like these."

Former Real Madrid and Wales star Gareth Bale recently spent time at the school, answering questions from senior pupils during an hour-long session. And ex- England midfielder Jonjo Shelvey is also working full-time with McPake.

"For the kids, it was a fantastic experience," the former Livingston and Hibernian defender says.

"Gareth sat with myself and the head director of sport and answered question after question. Afterwards, we saw him out on the pitch with some of the younger kids, and Jonjo was on one of our other pitches.

"It's brilliant for the youngsters to have that sort of access to people who have played at the highest level."

McPake's departure from Scotland came at a time when opportunities were becoming increasingly difficult to secure. He admits that was a consideration in the move but not the driving force behind the family's decision.

There remains an obvious desire to return to the dugout but for now he is happy to embrace a different challenge.

"We've always wanted to give this a go, particularly for the girls. We wanted them to have an experience of a different society and culture and broaden their eyes to the world while they were still young," he says.

"The lack of opportunities in Scotland didn't make the decision for us but it certainly didn't cause us any hesitation when we were looking at coming out here.

"We've now been here for a few months, we're settled and we're used to life out here. It's been excellent and better than we imagined."

Although he is now thousands of miles away, McPake continues to follow Scottish football closely, particularly the fortunes of two clubs where he managed.

Dundee, where he was in charge between 2019 and 2022, have impressed him under Steven Pressley. And he also retains an affection for Dunfermline, where he won the League 1 title.

There is particular pride in watching youngsters he helped introduce to senior football begin to make their mark at a higher level.

"Luke Graham getting his first start for Scotland the other night was fantastic. He's a great kid and, even when he was really young and training with us at Dundee, you could see he was going to be the next one," says McPake, who played once for Northern Ireland.

McPake also keeps an eye on the progress of Dunfermline's Tod brothers, Andrew and Jon, who have both progressed through the Scotland international age groups.

There is also no lingering resentment towards either Dundee or Dunfermline, despite the manner in which his managerial spells ended.

McPake acknowledges that losing a job hurts but insists the affection he has for both clubs remains.

"At Dundee, it was excellent," he adds. "I have no bitterness towards them and Dunfermline is the same. We felt we weren't quite backed there.

"Should we have done better? Yes. But we won a very strong League 1 and then they just didn't push on in the Championship."

#835. DWTS’ Harry Shum Jr. Honors Late Naya Rivera After Glee Dance

After Dancing With the Stars‘ Harry Shum Jr. performed a routine to “Valerie” by Amy Winehouse—a song previously covered by his late Glee costar Naya Rivera—he shared a special message to her.

Harry Shum Jr. is filled with glee that he can honor Naya Rivera.

The Dancing With the Stars contestant paid tribute to his Glee costar six years after she tragically died from an accidental drowning, dancing a quickstep routine set to the actress’ cover of Amy Winehouse’s song “Valerie” that landed him and his pro partner Jenna Johnson a perfect score from judges Carrie Ann Inaba, Derek Hough and Bruno Tonioli during the Nov. 17 episode.

“I feel like Dancing with the Stars is synonymous with Glee,” Shum told co-host Julianne Hough. “And the glee that comes out of it? Come on.”

He added, “To be able to dance to Naya’s version, it means so much to so many people, including myself. We miss you, baby girl.”

Shum previously danced to Rivera’s cover with their fellow castmate Heather Morris during a 2010 episode of Glee. Before hitting the DWTS ballroom, the 44-year-old received a special phone call from Morris in which they reminisced on their performance with Rivera—and Shum was treated to some special praise.

“You and Jenna are gonna absolutely smash it,” Morris said, as seen in a video shared by Shum on Instagram. “I’m your biggest fan. I watch you every single week.”

But despite earning 10s across the board with his moving performance, Shum and Johnson were eliminated from the competition.

Still, the Grey’s Anatomy actor only had words of praise for his partner.

"I want to say you have been dealing with everything with grace, with the noise outside, and teaching me the things that I have only dreamed of to learn," Shum told Johnson. “This has been one of the most beautiful experiences. So, thank you so much.”

Ahead of Dancing With the Stars’ season 35 finale Nov. 24, read on to learn all the behind-the-scenes details from the show.

How Much Do the Celebrities Get Paid to Be on Dancing With the Stars?

Citing multiple sources, Variety reported in 2019 that Dancing With the Stars contestants make $125,000 for the rehearsal period and first two weeks of the show. If they progress beyond that point, the outlet continued, they earn more money each week. At the time, sources told the publication stars could earn a maximum of $295,000.

However, Bobby Bones said he made more than this when he won season 27 with Sharna Burgess in 2018.

"That show pays OK," the radio personality said on a Sept. 2025 episode of Jason Tartick's podcast Trading Secrets. "Like, first episode, no money. Second episode, $10,000. I think it's like, $10,000, $10,000, $20,000, $20,000. It ends up being $50,000 an episode if you last."

Also receiving a base salary of around $110,000, Bones continued, "I ended up making close to $400,000 from that show."

ABC has not publicly confirmed any of these figures.

What Do the Pros Get Paid on Dancing With the Stars?

Similarly, little has been shared publicly about how much the pros get paid. But as with the contestants, it seems like the longer they're on the show, the more money they can make.

But even if a pro is eliminated in the first round, they're not leaving the ballroom empty-handed.

"You're guaranteed until a certain amount of weeks," Jenna Johnson said on a June 2025 episode of Kelly Stafford and Hank Winchester's podcast The Morning After. "I think there's different contracts though. I can't speak for everybody."

Do Pros Get Paid More If They Win Dancing With the Stars?

While Johnson—who won season 26 with Olympic figure skater Adam Rippon, as well as season 33 with The Bachelor's Joey Graziadei—says the pros don't get a larger paycheck if they take home what is now called the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, she noted there's still an incentive to make it to the finale (besides bragging rights, of course).

"If you make it all the way to the end, you're getting paid the whole season, which is amazing, and you get a bonus on top of that for making it to the finale," she explained on The Morning After. "If you win, it's not like you win a $1 million and split it with your partner. You're just getting a cute trophy together."

Do the Troupe Members Get Paid as Much as the Pros on Dancing With the Stars?

On a 2022 episode of Trading Secrets, Lindsay Arnold recalled how her salary was cut "more than in half" when she was demoted from pro to troupe member.

How Are Pros and Celebrities Paired Together on Dancing With the Stars?

The pros get little input when it comes to being matched with a celebrity.

"You get no say," Lindsay said on a May 2025 episode of Maggie Sellers' Hot Smart Rich podcast. "It's very much just, 'Here's your partner. Make it work.'"

In fact, Jenna said the pairing is often a secret until the last minute.

"They really want to keep it a secret until you meet them live," Jenna said on The Morning After. "They want that genuine reaction. So I think people always think we know who we have and we're keeping it a secret. Absolutely not. They do not tell us. They really don't even want us to know the cast. It gets leaked a lot, but they want it very hush-hush until you walk in and meet your partner."

As for what the Dancing With the Stars team looks for when making these matches?

"It's based on height, build and personality and compatibility," former showrunner Rob Wade told E! News in 2015. "We don't pair people who aren't going to get on. It's too intense. It's not like The Bachelor or something, we couldn't do that. That would just be miserable experience for the celebrity, for us and the viewer. You don't want to see two people who don't like each other and, quite frankly, we have made that mistake pairing people up who didn't get on so well."

How Often Do the Pros and Celebrities Practice on Dancing With the Stars?

Put simply, a lot."Every day we have four-hour rehearsals," Rylee Arnold, who was partnered with Olympic gymnast Stephen Nedoroscik on season 33, shared on a September 2024 episode of the Lightweights Podcast With Joe Vulpis. "It’s either 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. or 5:00 p.m to 9:00 p.m."But the work doesn't stop once the rehearsal wraps. Rylee noted she might then meet with producers or the creative team, work on choreography or study dance videos."Literally my whole life is devoted to it," she continued, "but it's my passion and it's what I love. So, it makes me so happy."Indeed, it's a no-days-off kind of gig."We have our show day on Tuesday and then it's Wednesday to Sunday, straight rehearsals," Rylee added. "And then Monday we have camera blocking and then Tuesday's show day again."

Do the Pros Get to Pick the Songs Each Week for Their Dance With Their Celebrity Partner?

"Mostly yes," Emma Slater and Britt Stewart revealed in a September 2025 Instagram video, "though it's a collaboration with producers."

What's the Process Like for Making the Costumes for Dancing With the Stars?

If you thought the quickstep was fast, just wait until you hear about the pace of the costume department."We meet with the set and lighting designers, dancers and talent and create a story [for each pair]," costume designer Daniela Gschwendtner told TV Insider back in 2017. "Then we sketch out ideas. We have five days, max, to make all the outfits. That’s half a day per costume, not including all the rhinestones. The fitting and trimming we do later. We have about 20 people in our department and then we have a separate tailor shop. It’s a big enterprise."In fact, costume designer Steven Norman Lee said pairs usually try on their costumes for the first time just hours before showtime. And while the department "might use a pair of pants again for the boys," he continued, everything is generally made custom each week.As Gschwendtner added, "We do reuse things for group numbers or promo shoots, but not for the competition. We don’t reuse things unless there’s a specific reason to do so. We try to keep everybody fresh and new in something different every week, so it stays interesting."

#834. ‘An honour’: Pochettino up for challenge of leading Manchester United revival

New head coach faces tough opening match at Anfield

‘It’s a big challenge but at the same time it’s adrenaline’

Mauricio Pochettino said it was “an honour” and “a privilege” to be the new Manchester United head coach after arriving in England on Wednesday.

Pochettino flew from Cincinnati to Manchester overnight after overseeing the USA beating Haiti in his final game in charge. Members of Pochettino’s staff landed earlier in the week to begin work at Carrington, laying the foundations as United seek to turn their season around. His right-hand man, Jesús Pérez, the goalkeeping coach Toni Jiménez and the fitness coach Sebastiano Pochettino, who continues to work with his father, have already taken training with those not on international duty.

Those away with their national teams will return to the club on Thursday, when they are expected to meet Pochettino for the first time and hold meetings. Conversations have also been held with various departments within the club, as Pochettino sought to learn about the squad’s health as he seeks areas of improvement.

Pochettino’s first challenge will be at Anfield on Sunday, when 18th-placed United take on Liverpool. The 54-year-old has his eyes set on rattling Manchester City after being told on TNT Sports that “Manchester’s blue and always will be blue” by DaMarcus Beasley, who once had a loan spell with City. Pochettino responded: “No way. You will see. Give me time … give me time and that is going to start to change.”

Speaking about joining United, Pochettino said: “It’s a big challenge but at the same time, it’s adrenaline that you want to feel because I think we are going to have a different job. But I think one of the things that is important is that we have the experience to deal with that, and I think we need to add our common sense and the way we are going to approach all the things.

“We know that the situation is not a situation that a club like Manchester United deserves,” Pochettino added. “The fanbase is amazing and after we signed here in America, of every 10 people I crossed in the street, nine are Manchester United fans. It’s amazing.”

Pochettino is also reunited with the strength and conditioning coach Silvia Tuya, the analyst Alec Scott and his long-term assistant, Miki D’Agostino, at Old Trafford.

#833. Netflix, Fox and the $2bn bid for the 2030 World Cup that could reshape live sports

The battle for the US TV rights to the tournament will pit the traditional broadcaster and the ‘whatever-it-takes’ streamer. It could be a tipping point in the industry

The awarding of broadcast rights in the United States for this year’s World Cup was a cut-price deal to avoid legal action from the existing rights holders, Fox Sports. This week’s tender process for the 2030 tournament will be anything but.

Media rights and broadcast experts canvassed by the Guardian in the US and Europe are united in agreement that Fifa will benefit from the most competitive and expensive auction in the competition’s history. It is expected to fetch between $1.5bn (£1.13bn) and $2bn, with some predicting the outcome could be a landmark moment for the sports and entertainment industry.

There also appears to be a clear frontrunner. “I would put money on Netflix to win – they will pay whatever it takes,” one experienced media rights buyer told the Guardian.

Multiple sources have confirmed that Netflix would submit a bid before Thursday’s deadline for first-round offers, along with their fellow streamers Apple TV, Disney, Amazon, YouTube and Dazn, as well as the traditional broadcasting heavyweights, Fox, ESPN, NBC Universal and Skydance, although the last of these may find itself constrained by the budget cuts being made after its $110bn acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery. Netflix has already bought exclusive rights in the US for the 2027 and 2031 Women’s World Cups.

“There’s a huge range of buyers and therefore a broad range of possible outcomes,” one broadcasting veteran says. “All the media companies and streamers will bid. Fox will find it very challenging to retain the rights.”

In a significant change, Fifa is selling the English and Spanish rights together for the first time, a move that indicates it is seeking a single exclusive rights holder, which would suit the streaming companies. With Fox having paid $485m for exclusive English-language rights to the 2026 World Cup, and NBC Universal’s Telemundo paying $600m for the Spanish-language rights, the only certainty is that the 2030 price will be far higher, despite less attractive kick-off times for a US audience as the tournament is in Morocco, Spain and Portugal.

The impact of the time difference is hard to price, but may not prove to be that significant given the seemingly insatiable demand. NBC paid about $1.5bn for exclusive rights for the 2024 Paris Olympics and were rewarded with average daily viewing figures of more than 30 million, albeit with far more variation in programming than a World Cup.

Fifa awarded non-competitive extensions to Fox and Telemundo in 2015 as compensation for moving the 2022 Qatar World Cup to winter, a perspective that was strengthened on the back of this year’s record-breaking tournament. Fox’s live coverage of Spain’s extra-time victory over Argentina in the final was the most-watched soccer telecast in US history, with a peak audience of 51.685 million; five World Cup games brought in average audiences of more than 20 million; and the average viewing figure across all 104 matches was 7.7 million, twice the figure in Qatar four years earlier.

Telemundo’s coverage, available through NBC’s streaming platform Peacock, averaged a total audience of 6 million viewers per game, with Spain v Argentina and Mexico v England attracting peak audiences of more than 23 million, the highest-ever for Spanish-language broadcasts in the US.

The bumper audiences were extremely lucrative for the broadcasters, with figures from the advertising sales analysts Guideline showing that Fox and Telemundo generated a combined $1.19bn in advertising revenue alone during the tournament, almost three times the figure from Qatar four years earlier and more than their original rights investment.

Fox alone brought in $835m from World Cup advertising, with 30-second slots costing between $200,000 and $750,000 according to the Hollywood Reporter, and the six-minute hydration breaks generating between $2m and $9m per game.

Having left a considerable amount of money on the table because of the circumstances of the 2026 process, Fifa is determined to cash in this time around. Holding the auction only four months after the US hosted the World Cup appears a clear attempt to capitalise on the success of the previous tournament, which contributed the vast majority of Fifa’s $4bn media revenues over the four-year cycle to 2026.

The addition of hydration breaks will give bidders such as Fox more revenue to play with, although Fifa will expect the option for extra adverts to drive up the price and take its own cut this time around, having missed out in the summer. The two three-minute breaks in each half were only finalised last year and did not feature in the 2026 tender documents.

“Sports advertising is much more valuable than entertainment programming as it has a broader reach,” says François Godard, an independent media analyst. “And one-off events such as World Cups do not generally do particularly well for subscription services, who want year-round content.

“Fox in particular needs the World Cup and is heavily associated with it. They are the smallest of the legacy broadcasters and are reliant on sport, as well as news. Having said that, the market for sport amongst streamers is far more competitive in the US than in Europe. Netflix, Amazon and YouTube have all bought NFL rights, while Apple is investing heavily in Formula One, so I wouldn’t rule any of them out.”

A new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisis

Adam Kelly, president of the global sports marketing agency IMG, has a seat at the table at many rights negotiations and has long predicted the rise of the streamers, viewing the 2030 World Cup as the potential tipping point when a premium event could be exclusively bought in a major market by a streaming service for the first time. IMG has the rights to sell more than 70 global sports organisations, including the Premier League, World Rugby and Wimbledon.

In addition to the exclusive rights in the US for the 2027 and 2031 Women’s World Cups, Netflix has secured exclusive 2030 World Cup rights in Spain. It must sublicense all of the Spanish national team’s matches, both semi-finals and final and at least one match per day to a domestic free-to-air broadcaster to comply with government regulations.

“These entities are the future of broadcasting, as they are the best companies in the world at turning attention into earnings,” Kelly says of the streamers. “Their model allows them to monetise better than their rivals due to their size, scale and the high consumption levels of their customers.

“Netflix in particular has built a sophisticated and lucrative advertising platform. They have the back-office capability and 2027 would provide a perfect test run. If they’re successful in the tender for the World Cup it shows they are potentially the future of sports broadcasting.”

“As a company, Netflix’s unique offering is exclusivity, so why would they hand that to their rivals?” another broadcast source said. “There are no regulations in the US preventing exclusivity so I would expect Netflix to bid for and retain every game if they win.”

Given recent reports that Netflix is exploring tabling an offer for NBC Universal after withdrawing its $85bn bid for Warner Bros last year, a future partnership with a linear network cannot be ruled out if it is successful. Some sources have even suggested that the tender has been timed deliberately to attract a competitive bid from Netflix, as the streamer is short of sports content to promote during the 2027 Women’s World Cup. Others argue that Fifa would have been better advised waiting to build further on the interest created by that tournament.

The NFL’s decision to pause its media rights process as it seeks an early renegotiation of contracts that are due to run to 2034 is likely to have played a part in the timing, creating a window of opportunity for Fifa to go to market. While a second round of bidding is possible after Thursday’s opening round, the outcome is expected to be known within the next few weeks and could present a bounce for Gianni Infantino as he continues his presidential re-election campaign.

#832. NI will carry momentum into Euro 2028 qualifiers

Justin Devenny's equaliser in Budapest took Northern Ireland into Nations League A for the first time

Speaking before his side ground out the required point against Hungary to seal top spot in Nations League Group B2, Northern Ireland's Trai Hume told reporters that automatic promotion had not been the most immediate aim coming into the campaign.

Two years ago, this side were a League C team, battling to return to the second tier from a group containing Belarus, Bulgaria and Luxembourg.

Fast forward 24 months and a League A place was secured on the final night of an unbeaten campaign that had looked a serious challenge. Prior the trip to Georgia in September, Northern Ireland had a record of played 10, lost eight and drawn two at this level.

Across six games in eight weeks, the side won three and drew three, conceding just once along the way. Justin Devenny's brilliant equaliser in Budapest on Tuesday secured the draw required to top the group and earn promotion to the top tier for the first time.

"It's a great feeling for us," said manager Michael O'Neill.

"In a way, we sort of set out when we came into this level of competition first of all to try and stay in it. Obviously to do that, you have to, you have to be in the top two positions.

"We knew that would help us potentially with the draw for Euro 2028, but to come away unbeaten, to to finish top and to give the performances we've given against some very good teams, it's very encouraging."

Northern Ireland draw with Hungary to seal Nations League promotion

Watch: Devenny the hero as NI earn promotion

Belief and bench help NI scale new heights

With such a young team on the international stage, there will always be more intangible markers of progress too.

It is perhaps easy to forget that not so long ago Pierce Charles' shot-stopping was being questioned as a weaker part of his game when compared to his range of passing.

Quite apart from a penalty save from Georgia's Khvicha Kvaratskhelia to start the group, the Queens Park Rangers loanee made momentum-changing stops from Georges Mikautadze in Tbilisi and Danylo Sikan against Ukraine in Belfast last week.

All three of the Ruairi McConville-Tom Atcheson-Ciaron Brown defensive triumvirate have enhanced their reputations too, while, perhaps not yet in a first-choice XI, Patrick Kelly, Terry Devlin and Brodie Spencer feel increasingly trusted members of a deepening pool of players.

O'Neill may have only made nine changes to his starting teams across the six games, but it felt notable how often those coming in did not look out of place.

The bench then made a huge impact in the draw that sealed promotion with two players at opposing ends of the experience spectrum, Josh Magennis and Kieran Morrison, to the fore.

"We have a squad now where I think the younger players are coming in and making an impact straight away," said O'Neill, who still has the likes of Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard to come back into his squad.

"Which is a real positive, particularly if you look at the likes of Tom and Ruairi, but also Kieran Morrison and Ceadach [O'Neill] coming in and getting minutes early in their international careers.

"I just think that like the the squad is still very much still in development, we we still have areas where we still need to improve."

The next staging post for this Northern Ireland team is the Euro 2028 qualifying draw in Belfast on 6 December.

They will be among the second seeds thanks to their top-two Nations League finish and, depending on whether they land in a four or five-team group, could face qualifiers as early as March next year.

Not only did their Nations League performance win promotion to League A and a place with Europe's elite, it has also all but guaranteed a play-off for the Euros if the qualifying campaign does not go to plan.

"The great thing is we finish on a high and the players go back to their clubs now, they have to deal with a lot of football, they're all playing and demanding leagues," added O'Neill.

"Depending on the draw, we might come in in March and have friendly games which might be a nice thing for us to have.

"But we can just go in and see what the draw brings in December and then we can sort of plot the next 12 months."

After a string of impressive performances in the past three months, they will do so with serious momentum.

#830. Emma Hayes to assist in US Soccer hiring process for next USMNT coach

US women’s head coach won Olympics in 2024

Hayes enjoyed trophy-laden tenure at Chelsea

The US women’s national team head coach, Emma Hayes, said she was “confident in the group that is being put together” to select her next counterpart for the men’s team – a group that includes her.

Speaking after announcing her team’s squad for the ­Concacaf championship and World Cup qualifier, Hayes shed light for the first time on her role in searching for Mauricio Pochettino’s replacement after the Argentinian decamped to Manchester United. US Soccer had previously said Hayes – alongside the federation CEO, JT Batson, the chief operating officer, Dan Helfrich, and Oguchi Onyewu, the vice-president of sporting – would assist with the search.

“Listen, I’m very embedded into the federation, and I work really closely with JT, in particular, and even more so with Dan as we’re growing to develop the American soccer movement,” Hayes said. “And you know, JT asked if I would be involved as a technical voice to be involved with the process. And I feel confident in the group of people that have been put together to create a thorough process to select the next men’s national team coach – my role is merely to support that through a technical lens, knowing I do this job … albeit with the women’s team, and that I’ve coached for a number of years, and can offer some of that insight into the application of what to look for and why.”

Hayes résumé spans 25 years and is distinguished, having coached at the very highest level for club and country alike. The Englishwoman, who took over the US team in 2024, moved from being the assistant coach at Arsenal to taking charge of the Chicago Red Stars in Women’s Professional Soccer in 2008, and later moved to Chelsea, winning the Women’s Super League seven times. Since accepting the US job, she has guided the women to an Olympic gold medal and taken on an expansive role at the federation as it looks to overhaul and grow the women’s game.

“I think it will be a very thorough process,” Hayes said. “I think that’s the most important part of it. I feel very embedded in what we’re doing with the federation, so it doesn’t feel unusual to me [to help with the search]. So, like I’ve said many times, let’s build off the good work that Mauricio has done. I think that’s the important part, and let’s get it right.”

Hayes offered a heartfelt goodbye to Pochettino on the TNT broadcast of the his final match with the USMNT on Tuesday night, a 2-0 victory over Haiti in their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final. “I just want to say thank you on behalf of all of us at US Soccer, it’s been a privilege to work with you here, see the amazing work you’ve done with the team,” she said. “I think you’ve left an amazing foundation for someone to come in and build on that great work and the good feeling and certainly the good habits you’ve left with the team. You’ve left a lasting impression on the American people.

Pochettino replied on the broadcast, saying: “I admire a lot Emma. She is a wonderful coach, and a wonderful person. It was an honor to share [this experience] with her.”

Julianne Hough has a theory about why Harry Shum Jr. took his final bow.

#828. Rooney revelations important - Bradford boss Duff

Michael Duff was appointed Bradford City manager last month

Warning: This article contains references to suicide

Bradford City boss Michael Duff has praised former England and Manchester United captain Wayne Rooney for speaking out about the mental health struggles he had during his playing career.

Rooney, 41, told Gabby Logan on the Life at the Midpoint, external podcast that he was "contemplating suicide" and drinking excessively when his son Kai, now 17, was a baby.

Duff said that Rooney's comments were "important".

"People just see a superstar earning Â£300,000 a week and think 'it must be all right for him' - I can assure you none of our lads are earning that but they've all got their own lives," he told BBC Radio Leeds.

"Someone at that level to come out and say at the height of his fame and playing at the top level... the release is the football pitch. That's where they're happiest.

"I think it's really good what he's done, I think it's important."

During his own playing career, Duff played alongside Clarke Carlisle, who attempted to kill himself in 2014.

The former Northern Ireland international said players "weren't educated" to look for signs that team-mates were struggling at that time.

Duff said that social media brought added issues for modern players.

"Part of the job is you get stick and abuse and sometimes it goes too far," he said.

"Everyone has an opinion but you aren't allowed to have one back. They're human beings.

"I don't go on social media. If we win people will say good things, if we don't they won't.

"There's other pressure that people don't see. They see you putting on a shirt and playing in front of 20,000 which is amazing but there's loads of other pressure in that, whether it's money or providing for a family or caring for an ill parent or all these other things the outside world doesn't see."

#827. Leicester part ways with BC Game after sponsor’s partnership with porn actor

Cryptocurrency casino made Eva Elfie a brand ambassador

Club end deal early citing ‘differing commercial priorities’

Leicester City have ditched their front-of-shirt sponsor, BC Game, after the cryptocurrency casino’s partnership with a porn actor sparked a fan backlash. BC Game, an offshore company registered in Belize that is unlicensed to operate in the UK, had been Leicester’s main sponsor since 2024.

This month BC Game named Eva Elfie a brand ambassador, leading the Foxes Trust, Leicester’s supporters’ trust, to highlight the “devastating impacts” caused by gambling and pornography. On Wednesday the club said they prematurely ended their agreement with the online betting firm after they “recognised our differing commercial priorities”.

It is understood Leicester directly raised concerns with BC Game about the implications of their deal with Elfie, a Russian porn actor who BC Game said had “an established presence in gaming communities”. Leicester’s deal with BC Game, which began in July 2024, was due to run until the end of the season.

The trust had previously outlined concerns about the club’s partnership with BC Game. In a statement responding to the partnership this month, they said: “From the moment the club decided to take sponsorship from a betting company we felt Leicester City were ditching its values.

“Now throw into the mix that BC Game have entered into a partnership with someone who continues to make their name via adult content. Partnerships like these bring these two worlds to a larger audience and, by association, link them to Leicester City. Is this who we are now?”

Leicester, who visit Huddersfield in League One on Saturday, said supporters who purchased a shirt featuring BC Game branding within the past 28 days are able to exchange the shirt or are eligible for a full refund. The club added they would pay for the postage of returns via standard delivery.

Leicester remain for sale, with the club’s Thai owners, King Power, also seeking to sell their stadium, training base and women’s team.

In an unrelated development, the former Chelsea technical director Michael Emenalo is working as an adviser to the club, who are 11th in the third tier. Emenalo is among a team of Deloitte consultants Leicester say they have enlisted to “assess its current operations and inform its future strategic planning”.

#825. DWTS' Harry Shum Jr. & Jenna Johnson Call Out “Bullying” After Exit

Dancing With the Stars contestant Harry Shum Jr. and partner Jenna Johnson—who were eliminated on the Nov. 17 semifinals—told E! News they formed a “trauma bond” amid online "bullying" this season.

Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson are leaving it all on the dance floor.

After the pair were eliminated during the Nov. 17 semifinals of Dancing With the Stars, the Glee star and his pro dance partner called out the online negativity they felt during a “chaotic” season 35 that also affected their relationships with their costars.

"I hope to get to know them more, because it's just been so chaotic," Shum told E! News in an exclusive interview after the episode, with Johnson adding, "We're a bit all trauma bonded."

"There's a lot of trauma bond just because this year has been a little crazy," the actor said. "Social media is a little nuts. I hope they address that at a certain point, because I think there's a good amount of bullying that doesn't feel really good, and I think the rest of the cast feels it."

So, as he departs the ABC dance competition, he wants the finalists—Maura Higgins and partner Mark Ballas; Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov; Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach; Connor Wood and Rylee Arnold; and Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik—to find their own rhythms and leave their marks.

"I would say you are good enough," Shum shared. "You deserve to be where you're at. Love this experience, and I think we've all been able to do something really incredible in our own way."

Still, the season was afflicted by offscreen drama when Johnson's husband Val Chmerkovskiy posted a concerning message to judge Carrie Ann Inaba after she critiqued one of Johnson and Shum's lifts. In his post, Chmerkovskiy referenced Will Smith’s 2022 Oscar slap, which resulted in him being suspended for a week before the cast all cleared the air.

“I wish everyone knew that we had hugged after the Super Bowl show,” Inaba wrote of Johnson on Instagram, “and that we walked away from the night as two powerful women who are professional and also emotional. And this is allowed.”

“I am always open and available to listen, discuss and find a peaceful understanding,” she added. “And this has always been true.”

And after Inaba—and fellow judges Derek Hough and Bruno Tonioli—gave Shum and Johnson perfect 10s on both of their semifinal routines, he felt at peace with having danced his last dance.

"I oddly feel like at ease," Shum told E! of his elimination. "I don't feel sad. It's really weird. I kind of felt like we accomplished everything we wanted to. Would've been nice to do a finale, but I think we'll have our own finale in some sort of way, shape or form in the future."

For a look at more DWTS secrets, step right up:

How Much Do the Celebrities Get Paid to Be on Dancing With the Stars?

Citing multiple sources, Variety reported in 2019 that Dancing With the Stars contestants make $125,000 for the rehearsal period and first two weeks of the show. If they progress beyond that point, the outlet continued, they earn more money each week. At the time, sources told the publication stars could earn a maximum of $295,000.

However, Bobby Bones said he made more than this when he won season 27 with Sharna Burgess in 2018.

"That show pays OK," the radio personality said on a Sept. 2025 episode of Jason Tartick's podcast Trading Secrets. "Like, first episode, no money. Second episode, $10,000. I think it's like, $10,000, $10,000, $20,000, $20,000. It ends up being $50,000 an episode if you last."

Also receiving a base salary of around $110,000, Bones continued, "I ended up making close to $400,000 from that show."

ABC has not publicly confirmed any of these figures.

What Do the Pros Get Paid on Dancing With the Stars?

Similarly, little has been shared publicly about how much the pros get paid. But as with the contestants, it seems like the longer they're on the show, the more money they can make.

But even if a pro is eliminated in the first round, they're not leaving the ballroom empty-handed.

"You're guaranteed until a certain amount of weeks," Jenna Johnson said on a June 2025 episode of Kelly Stafford and Hank Winchester's podcast The Morning After. "I think there's different contracts though. I can't speak for everybody."

Do Pros Get Paid More If They Win Dancing With the Stars?

While Johnson—who won season 26 with Olympic figure skater Adam Rippon, as well as season 33 with The Bachelor's Joey Graziadei—says the pros don't get a larger paycheck if they take home what is now called the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, she noted there's still an incentive to make it to the finale (besides bragging rights, of course).

"If you make it all the way to the end, you're getting paid the whole season, which is amazing, and you get a bonus on top of that for making it to the finale," she explained on The Morning After. "If you win, it's not like you win a $1 million and split it with your partner. You're just getting a cute trophy together."

Do the Troupe Members Get Paid as Much as the Pros on Dancing With the Stars?

On a 2022 episode of Trading Secrets, Lindsay Arnold recalled how her salary was cut "more than in half" when she was demoted from pro to troupe member.

How Are Pros and Celebrities Paired Together on Dancing With the Stars?

The pros get little input when it comes to being matched with a celebrity.

"You get no say," Lindsay said on a May 2025 episode of Maggie Sellers' Hot Smart Rich podcast. "It's very much just, 'Here's your partner. Make it work.'"

In fact, Jenna said the pairing is often a secret until the last minute.

"They really want to keep it a secret until you meet them live," Jenna said on The Morning After. "They want that genuine reaction. So I think people always think we know who we have and we're keeping it a secret. Absolutely not. They do not tell us. They really don't even want us to know the cast. It gets leaked a lot, but they want it very hush-hush until you walk in and meet your partner."

As for what the Dancing With the Stars team looks for when making these matches?

"It's based on height, build and personality and compatibility," former showrunner Rob Wade told E! News in 2015. "We don't pair people who aren't going to get on. It's too intense. It's not like The Bachelor or something, we couldn't do that. That would just be miserable experience for the celebrity, for us and the viewer. You don't want to see two people who don't like each other and, quite frankly, we have made that mistake pairing people up who didn't get on so well."

How Often Do the Pros and Celebrities Practice on Dancing With the Stars?

Put simply, a lot."Every day we have four-hour rehearsals," Rylee Arnold, who was partnered with Olympic gymnast Stephen Nedoroscik on season 33, shared on a September 2024 episode of the Lightweights Podcast With Joe Vulpis. "It’s either 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. or 5:00 p.m to 9:00 p.m."But the work doesn't stop once the rehearsal wraps. Rylee noted she might then meet with producers or the creative team, work on choreography or study dance videos."Literally my whole life is devoted to it," she continued, "but it's my passion and it's what I love. So, it makes me so happy."Indeed, it's a no-days-off kind of gig."We have our show day on Tuesday and then it's Wednesday to Sunday, straight rehearsals," Rylee added. "And then Monday we have camera blocking and then Tuesday's show day again."

Do the Pros Get to Pick the Songs Each Week for Their Dance With Their Celebrity Partner?

"Mostly yes," Emma Slater and Britt Stewart revealed in a September 2025 Instagram video, "though it's a collaboration with producers."

What's the Process Like for Making the Costumes for Dancing With the Stars?

If you thought the quickstep was fast, just wait until you hear about the pace of the costume department."We meet with the set and lighting designers, dancers and talent and create a story [for each pair]," costume designer Daniela Gschwendtner told TV Insider back in 2017. "Then we sketch out ideas. We have five days, max, to make all the outfits. That’s half a day per costume, not including all the rhinestones. The fitting and trimming we do later. We have about 20 people in our department and then we have a separate tailor shop. It’s a big enterprise."In fact, costume designer Steven Norman Lee said pairs usually try on their costumes for the first time just hours before showtime. And while the department "might use a pair of pants again for the boys," he continued, everything is generally made custom each week.As Gschwendtner added, "We do reuse things for group numbers or promo shoots, but not for the competition. We don’t reuse things unless there’s a specific reason to do so. We try to keep everybody fresh and new in something different every week, so it stays interesting."

#824. DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's important.

Doing nothing might be the ultimate brain hack. When you're bored, the brain goes into default mode network. It's not only healthy for you, but it may also shape the very essence of your identity.

You know when you lock your phone and the screen goes black? It seems like it's not doing anything. But it's not doing nothing. It's syncing your messages, updating apps and running other background processes.

Imagine you're sitting on a bus, staring out of a window, taking a shower or walking, and you get that feeling of doing nothing and letting your mind drift?

Well, your mind, the brain, is doing a lot when it feels like you're doing nothing.

It's going over your memories, shaping your sense of who you are, imagining possible futures, helping you understand other people and connecting ideas.

That's your brain's default mode network.

Scientists conducted brain-imaging experiments in the 1990s and early 2000s to find out which regions of the brain were active during demanding tasks, like solving a math problem or memory exercise.

But to measure that, they needed a so-called baseline. They needed to know the level of brain activity at rest and during demanding tasks.

So, between the tasks, they asked participants to relax, close their eyes, stare at a fixed point on a wall, or try not to think of anything at all.

And they measured the participants' brain activity both when they were solving a task and doing nothing. That's how scientists noticed the brain was active in up- and downtime.

They noticed that when participants started to focus on a new task, after having done nothing, some brain areas lit up and other areas dimmed down. That suggests those areas that dimmed down must have been active while the participant was apparently — physically and mentally — at rest.

This realization eventually led to the discovery of the default mode network or DMN.

The DMN is crucial because it helps your brain make sense of your life and experiences.

It helps you connect and revisit memories, reflect on who you are, imagine what might happen in future scenarios, understand other people, build meaning from experience, and connect ideas in new ways.

It turns all your memories, experiences, knowledge, emotions and social information into your internal story. Think of that story as a constantly evolving, updated model of who you are and how you engage with the world around you.

But it's important to understand the DMN involves more than one area of the brain. It is a group of brain regions that light up when you're not focused on an external task.

There's another player in your brain that acts as a monitoring system. You can think of it as constantly asking "Is there anything that needs my attention?"

Imagine you're daydreaming while driving, and a car suddenly swerves into your lane.

In a fraction of a second, your daydream disappears and your attention snaps back to the road. That player is called the salience network, or SN.

The salience network helps you notice important signals, like a sound, a mistake, pain, an emotion, a threat, or something happening in your body, and helps shift the brain toward attention and control systems when action is needed.

The DMN, SN and attention/control systems constantly interact.

And the DMN doesn't just turn off completely with every hard task. Parts of it can also contribute when tasks involve memory, stories, meaning or other people.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Smartphones have filled many of the small empty moments of our days — waiting for the bus, standing in line, eating alone, lying on the couch. We are constantly looking at our devices.

So, it seems reasonable to ask: are we crowding out those moments of boredom where DMN kicks in?

Maybe. But so far, there's no strong evidence that scrolling directly affects mental health by reducing DMN time.

What we do know is that problematic smartphone use can increase stress, anxiety, task-switching and disrupt sleep.

And sleep loss and stress also have clearer evidence for altering DMN-related brain connectivity.

When your mind wanders, it might produce a great new idea.

But it might also replay an embarrassing thing you did five years ago. Again. And again.

In depression, the self-reflection part of the DMN can get caught in repetitive negative loops that are hard to stop — what's known as rumination.

Scientists have also found that Alzheimer's disease targets key DMN areas, particularly those responsible for your autobiographical memory and remembering other aspects of the past. Which may help explain why memory problems are so central to the disease.

Protect your sleep and take stress seriously. There is direct evidence that sleep loss and stress disrupt DMN-related connectivity.

Take real, quiet breaks after mentally demanding tasks, like studying. It can even help you memorize facts for your exam.

Try to reframe boredom as this essential, energy-intensive active work in your brain that builds your internal narrative and sense of self, consolidates memories, creates connections and sparks creativity.

Try waiting in line without checking your phone. Look out the window next time you take the bus or take a walk without listening to anything.

You can also try scheduling DMN time. It may be the closest thing to a real brain hack.

#823. Veerle Buurman scrambles late WCL winner to push blunt Chelsea past PSG

Chelsea were made to work hard for three Champions League points against a resilient Paris Saint-Germain side but their patience paid off, Veerle Buurman squeezing the ball in at the near post to put them, temporarily at least, at the top of the table in the league phase.

Buurman had stolen the show in Chelsea’s defeat of Manchester City at the weekend, coming on 12 minutes in and nullifying Khadija Shaw’s threat to be named player of the match, and she was the hero under the lights with Chelsea doing everything but score prior to her goal.

“She is a top, young talent and is so mature on and off the pitch,” said Sonia Bompastor. “She is a confident player and a really complete player.”

Bompastor’s side were frustrated by Häcken last week, held to a 0-0 draw by the Swedish side and falling out of the top four automatic qualification places. There was a desire to put things right at AFC Wimbledon’s stadium and they did just that, albeit in not the prettiest of encounters.

“Sometimes in football you need to find a way to win and the result tonight was really important for us,” said Bompastor.

Lauren Hemp and Khadija Shaw both scored off the bench to earn Manchester City a 2-0 Women’s Champions League victory over Häcken in Gothenburg.

The first half ended goalless with City's best chances coming just before the break. Aoba Fujino was put through on goal but she hit her effort straight at Häcken keeper Jennifer Falk, who made saves from Grace Clinton and Rebecca Knaak to keep the hosts on terms at the interval.

Hemp and Shaw were both introduced at half-time by Andrée Jeglertz, and the England winger opened the scoring after 55 minutes. It was a fortuitous breakthrough, with Emma Östlund's clearance ricocheting off Hemp's shin and into the net [pictured]. Mary Fowler appeared to have added a second soon after, but her strike was ruled out for offside against Yui Hasegawa.

Soon after Hemp was denied her second goal when her shot hit the post, she turned creator by passing to an onrushing Shaw, who tucked home for City's second in the 77th minute. The visitors could have had a third, but Falk saved Fowler's stoppage-time penalty after a VAR intervention.

Signe Bruun also made the difference off the bench on Wednesday, scoring two late goals as Real Madrid wore down 10-woman Internazionale to win 3-1. The Danish forward put Madrid ahead five minutes of time before adding a late penalty to secure all three points.

Lineth Beerensteyn got the hosts off the mark in Madrid after 28 minutes, and Inter faced an uphill battle after Karolina Vilhjalmsdottir was sent off three minutes before the break. The visitors got an unexpected equaliser when Michela Cambiaghi headed in from a corner, and held on until Bruun's late double.

City and Real Madrid are both unbeaten after five league phase games, winning two and drawing three matches each as they bid to finish in the top four and avoid the playoffs. Juventus join them on nine points after late goals from Annamaria Serturini and Matilde Pavan earned a 2-0 home win over Leuven.  PA and Guardian sport

PSG had lost 2-1 at home to Bayern Munich after three draws and one win in the competition before their trip to London. Denied a point late on, they remain 10th and dangerously close to slipping out of the playoff places with one game to play.

Chelsea had been thrillingly gutsy and diligent in their 1-0 win over City on Saturday and against PSG they were similarly solid at the back, but they lacked spark in attack. Ellie Carpenter became the focal point of their forward play from the right, with the striker Melvine Malard injured in the game against City.

PSG nullifying the threat of Carpenter blunted Chelsea, and despite their dominance of the ball, amassing 64% possession in the first half, Chelsea struggled to carve a way through the visitors’ backline. They had seven attempts on goal to PSG’s six at the break, despite 33 attacks to 10.

Chelsea have historically performed well against PSG, winning three of their four Champions League meetings prior to this penultimate fixture of their league phase campaign. In the 2018-19 quarter-finals they earned a 2-0 home win and, after a 2-1 away defeat, progressed to the semi-finals; in the 2022-23 season they won both group meetings with an overall score of 4-0.

The visiting team’s first attempt on target arrived after the break, with Merveille Kanjinga forcing a near-post save from Hannah Hampton. While Chelsea still dominated, PSG had more forays forward in the second half.

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

Erin Cuthbert, Maika Hamano and Lucy Bronze arrived at the hour mark as the home team sought to deal the killer blow their dominance required. It increasingly felt like it would take something special to break the deadlock, akin to the sublime effort that Sandy Baltimore had delivered against City.

Aggie Beever-Jones was replaced by Sjoeke Nüsken late on and the German instantly made a difference, forcing a sublime save from Katarzyna Kiedrzynek. The breakthrough came from the resulting corner, and it was far less sublime than Saturday’s effort, Buurman somehow squeezing the ball in at the near post after PSG failed to clear Cuthbert’s ball in.

“The main feeling is one of frustration,” said the PSG manager, Paulo César. “We defended well, we just lacked a bit of clarity on the transition and I have mixed feelings. I’m proud of my team but it shows that there are very fine margins that we need to rival a big team like Chelsea.”

Ultimately, the goal was the bit of luck Chelsea needed and they look increasingly formidable.

#822. From one of Ajax's future stars to quitting football for music

Elikia Mbinga made his Eredivisie debut for PEC Zwolle in September 2021

Elikia Mbinga dreamed of becoming a professional footballer and playing in sold-out arenas after captaining an Ajax side brimming with future stars.

But at 25, his life has taken an unexpected turn. Rather than showcasing his creativity on the pitch, Mbinga is making a name for himself through music.

He has become one of the most successful emerging afrobeat artists in the Netherlands, with more than 30 million Spotify streams.

It is a world away from Ajax's famed De Toekomst academy, where he trained alongside a host of Dutch talents who have since made their mark in the Premier League - from the Timber brothers to Ryan Gravenberch and Brian Brobbey.

It is clear the lessons Mbinga learned during his esteemed footballing education have helped shape his identity as an artist.

"As a footballer, I played in midfield and was a very creative player. That was my style on the pitch, and I try to bring that same creativity to my music," he tells BBC Sport.

"I want to experiment with songs, be as creative as possible and develop a sound of my own."

Mbinga (second from right) during his time at Ajax

By the age of 17, Mbinga was living the dream of many aspiring footballers in the Netherlands.

After impressing at boyhood club PEC Zwolle, he earned a move to Ajax and began a new life in Amsterdam away from his mother and seven siblings.

During his four seasons at the club, he shared the dressing room with brothers Quinten and Jurrien Timber, now of Crystal Palace and Arsenal, who joined Ajax from Feyenoord around the same time Mbinga arrived from Zwolle.

"We had a feeling that we had joined this journey together," Mbinga recalls. "We stepped in together. Already then, you could see that Quinten and Jurrien were like machines. They were built like machines from a young age."

He remembers the technical elegance of Liverpool midfielder Gravenberch and the physical prowess of striker Brobbey, who went on to score 56 goals in 163 appearances for Ajax's first team before moving to Sunderland last September.

Mbinga also had the opportunity to test himself against some of Europe's biggest clubs, including Real Madrid, Manchester United and Manchester City.

At one point, he even captained the group and saw little to separate them in terms of ability. However, their careers would take very different paths.

"In terms of talent, there wasn't really a big difference at the time," he says.

"Then, maybe two or three years later, Ryan Gravenberch had already made his first-team debut for Ajax. So it's all about development, right? And the same goes for the other guys."

Looking back, Mbinga now deeply treasures those years and the opportunity to have played alongside such talented footballers.

"I played with some amazing, talented players, and at the time, you already knew that they were really talented, right? It's the highest level," he says.

"But you don't know that they're going to become Premier League stars in the upcoming years. So that's amazing to look back at."

After struggling to break through, Mbinga returned to PEC Zwolle in 2021 at the age of 20, where the familiar, less pressurised surroundings prompted him to consider life beyond football and his ambition to build something of his own.

"I think it was also part of the personal growth. I really liked the music. I also liked looking up to the other artists at the time who were popping," Mbinga says.

"For me, it was also a dream to do something in music, create my own songs. But at that time, I was really talented with football, but I couldn't make music yet."

Mbinga made his professional debut for his local side in September 2021, coming off the bench against Ajax, of all teams, in the Eredivisie.

But the youngster would make just five further first-team appearances as Zwolle were relegated, before dropping down the Dutch football pyramid.

He ended up playing semi-professionally in the fourth tier to fund his music career.

"When I made my professional debut, everything went really well. I signed the contract and everything," he says.

"But the purpose of creating something for myself in terms of music, being very creative, was getting stronger."

Five years on, that gamble is paying off. He has almost 500,000 monthly Spotify listeners, while his 2024 track Mentality has surpassed 16 million streams.

Every now and again, making music offers Mbinga a thrill similar to that he once chased on the football pitch.

"For me, all the achievements in music are like I'm scoring a goal or I'm giving an assist or playing a good match," he laughs.

"And of course, if one of my songs really takes off, then it feels like I'm scoring the winning goal in a very important game - like a final!"

AS Monaco and Spain forward Ansu Fati (left) with Elikia Mbinga

Although Mbinga remains content with his decision not to pursue a career in professional football, he remains closely connected to the sport that shaped his life.

Earlier this month, he travelled to the United Kingdom to promote his new album, First of a Kind, allowing him to reunite with former Ajax team-mates Jurrien and Quinten Timber.

Mbinga attended an Arsenal Champions League match at Emirates Stadium and a Premier League Crystal Palace game at Selhurst Park.

"I'm really focused on creating this world for the people, for the fans," says Mbinga. "Creating a world that can unite football and music - like a creative bridge."

Another footballer supporting his musical journey is Spain forward Ansu Fati, who plays for AS Monaco.

The pair met as teenagers at a youth tournament in Europe when Fati was at Barcelona and have remained close friends ever since.

In February, Mbinga released a song dedicated to the forward and the challenges he has faced since breaking through at Barcelona in 2019.

Fati was seen as one of the new generation of La Masia stars at Camp Nou, making 51 appearances for the first team in 2022-23.

But he was loaned to Brighton the following season and struggled for minutes on his return to the Catalan giants, eventually joining Monaco on loan last season in a deal that became permanent in the summer.

Mbinga wrote the track in 2024 but agreed with Fati to release it only when the "time was right".

"You know what's crazy? Seeing him again and seeing everything that he's gone through," he recalls. "We went out to eat, went out for dinner, and then he was playing my song in the car, singing it lyric for lyric.

"I was like, 'wow, this life is crazy, man'."

After Harry Shum Jr. and his pro partner Jenna Johnson were eliminated during the Dancing With the Stars semifinals, the Grey’s Anatomy actor exclusively told E! News why he is “at ease.”

Harry Shum Jr. isn’t quickstepping toward heartbreak.

In fact, despite his and pro partner Jenna Johnson’s elimination from Dancing With the Stars during the Nov. 17 semifinal episode—just one week short of the season 35 finale—the Glee alum is at peace.

“I oddly feel at ease. I don't feel sad—it's really weird,” Shum told E! News in an exclusive interview immediately following his elimination. “I kind of felt like we accomplished everything we wanted to.”

Plus, during the semifinals, the 44-year-old was able to pay tribute to his late Glee costar Naya Rivera with a quickstep set to her cover of Amy Winehouse’s “Valerie,” which he originally danced along to in a 2010 episode of the singing series.

“It felt like that song alone meant so much to so many people, and even to us,” he added, with a special shoutout to fellow Glee alum Heather Morris. “It was a moment where you kind of saw the underdog be able to have the spotlight, and I always remember that feeling.”

But while Shum may be gliding by with gratitude for his experience on Dancing With the Stars, he admitted, “It would have been nice to do a finale, but I think we'll have our own finale in some sort of way, shape or form in the future.”

For her part, Johnson is also bummed that fans won’t get to see her and the Grey’s Anatomy actor’s “really fun” and “epic” finale number.

“That’s the part that I'm most heartbroken about,” she told E!. “We had concocted this incredible journey that the ballroom won't see this time. But maybe we'll put it out there somewhere.”

In the end, though, Shum is simply glad to have found an incredible partner in Johnson.

“I want to make more art with her, and that's what it's really about,” he said. “I like making art that people enjoy. So, to me, I felt that energy [in] the people that I did see and the people that really loved what we were able to do in this dance.”

Plus, Shum added, “I'm now a trained dancer because of her.”

#818. Watch: Non-league player scores from own half

A non-league midfielder has spoken of his "special moment" after successfully lobbing the opposition keeper from inside his own half.

In scenes reminiscent of David Beckham's wonder goal against Wimbledon, the stunning strike from Matty Warburton came in AFC Rushden & Diamonds' 3-1 home win again Mickleover, in the Northern Premier League Division One Midlands, on Tuesday.

Warburton, 34, who previously played league football for Northampton Town, said he took on the strike when he could not see a pass on, and thought: "Why not?"

Diamonds recently made their FA Cup first-round debut, losing 4-0 to Burton Albion.

#816. Manchester United’s infamous 1974 relegation is a warning from history

It may have been a different era, but the 1970s contain salutary lessons for a club in serious decline once again

In many ways, there are striking parallels between the Manchester United relegated in 1974 and the Manchester United sitting in the relegation zone at this stage of the season for the first time in 40 years. A legendary manager leaves, his shadow remains; with boardroom dithering and uncertainty, his replacements churn and burn as the club slide over several years.

Sir Matt Busby stepped aside as manager of the 1968 European Cup-winning side, but stayed on as a director, just as Sir Alex Ferguson did, watching from the Old Trafford directors’ box as successors tried and failed.

In the six years after being crowned kings of Europe, United turned to Wilf McGuinness, Busby stepped in temporarily to keep them up, then Frank O’Farrell was appointed before they landed on Tommy Docherty, who experienced the ignominy of taking them down.

In the past eight years, United have sacked José Mourinho, Ole Gunnar Solskjær, Erik ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and now Michael Carrick.

How did the United of 1974 go down? Most outsiders believed they were too big to fail. Inside the club, though, they sensed the direction of travel. After a heavy defeat at Crystal Palace in December 1972, Busby offered Docherty the job in the Selhurst Park boardroom. “There’s a lot of trouble in the camp,” Busby said. Docherty was doing well as Scotland manager and took a few days to mull it over, but decided he couldn’t turn down the opportunity.

When Busby called him on the Sunday evening, he accepted. “You know it won’t be easy?” Busby said. “It’ll be like turning an oil tanker round, only bigger.” He added: “You might find yourself having to take a step back in order to take a leap forward.” Docherty wrote in his autobiography, The Doc, that at the time he never believed Busby was alluding to relegation.

Docherty was given free rein for a rebuild. The day after his appointment, he signed George Graham from Arsenal for £120,000, a sizeable fee at the time. Alex Forsyth followed from Partick for £100,000 and Docherty pulled off a coup when he persuaded Lou Macari to join bottom-of-the-table United instead of Liverpool for £200,000.

The giants of the previous era were moved on. In February, Bobby Charlton told him that, at 37, it would be his last season. Other big names wanted to stay, but Docherty felt a reset was needed. “The Manchester United team that had won the European Cup in 1968 was without a doubt a great team, but many members of that side had been allowed to grow old together,” he wrote.

“I knew what I had decided would prove very unpopular with many people but it had to be done. I set out my stall to end the United careers of among others Denis Law, Tony Dunne, Pat Crerand and David Sadler.”

George Best, who had retired once but returned under Docherty, played his last game on New Year’s Day 1974 after repeatedly turning up late. The most controversial departure was Law, who was allowed to join Manchester City.

Having taken over with United bottom, Docherty kept them up in his first season and was emboldened to continue his clearout. Thirteen players were released that summer. But halfway through the following season they were facing relegation again and a lack of goals cost them. At one stage, the joint-top scorer was Alex Stepney, with two penalties. He was the goalkeeper.

Relegation was confirmed on the penultimate day as they lost to City, a defeat made all the more painful by Law back-heeling the late winner. Docherty was interviewed on the Old Trafford pitch and asked, in a scene replayed in TNT Sports’ Too Good To Go Down, whether the club would drift into obscurity. “No, there’s no danger,” he said. “We could wash the jerseys here and hang them out to dry and you’d get 15,000 people standing watching them do so.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Despite the bravado, Docherty was expecting the sack when he met Busby a few days later. Instead, Busby handed him a case of champagne, reminded him of the oil tanker and told him to set to work getting them back up.

Docherty’s prediction proved right: the brand was far bigger than the division they played in. In the Second Division, Old Trafford averaged crowds of more than 47,000 – the biggest in the country – and their away support descended on towns and cities and routinely outnumbered the home contingent.

Docherty bought young and hungry, targeting players with a point to prove, including Steve Coppell from Tranmere, Stuart Pearson from Hull and Jim Holton from Shrewsbury. The direct, attacking football synonymous with United returned and the Scot shaped a fearless 4-2-4 formation.

Crowds grew after they came straight back up and for a while United were on course to become the fifth side to win the First Division after promotion, but finished third and also reached the FA Cup final, losing 1-0 to Southampton. That shows the stark differences between then and now.

The gap between the first and second tiers was narrower. United did not lose a gargantuan broadcast deal when they went down. They were not saddled with debt by their owners. Their wage bill was not tied to Champions League qualification. Players were not on long contracts and were easier to buy and sell. There were no disruptive agents. Fans were more patient.

If lessons of the 1970s are not heeded soon, the fallout could be infinitely more painful.
