#750. ‘Sentimental Value’ Casting Guru Recalls Meta Stellan Skarsgard and Elle Fanning Experience

Yngvill Haga also discussed her rapport with Joachim Trier and Fanning's Oscar nomination during an appearance in the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival's market program.

You may not know Yngvill Haga by name. But the likes of Stellan Skarsgard and her regular collaborator Joachim Trier do. And you very likely know the Norwegian’s work as a casting director on the likes of Trier’s Oscar winner Sentimental Value, The Worst Person in the World and Thelma.

On Wednesday, she took the spotlight, of sorts, herself in an appearance at the Industry@Tallinn & Baltic Event (ITBE), the market of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) in Estonia, whose 30th edition runs through this weekend. Related Stories Movies He Lives in Madonna's Old Mansion. Now He's Made a Movie About Cambodian Genocide Music Boy George on His Controversial Israel Trip, Ed Sheeran and the Friends He Lost Along the Way

Asked about how she first met Trier, Haga shared: “His producer at that time texted or called me. ‘Do you want to have a coffee with him?’ I didn’t know him, and I always want to meet directors that I don’t know, so yeah, sure. I don’t know who has seen Sentimental Value, but we met at Lorry’s, the restaurant where the father and daughter have this talk [in the film]. Joachim loves that place, and he pitched me for a film called Thelma.”

The casting expert not only liked the film but also their connection. “I immediately liked his pitch and also our way of communicating, talking together,” Haga said. “He hadn’t worked with a casting director before; he had put people together to do his casting, but now he wanted to try out something else, and so it started from there.”

Of course, Trier wrote Sentimental Value with Renate Reinsve in mind. “When I first met Joachim [about the film], he pitched the story again, and he said, in a kind of nervous way, ‘I’m starting to think about Stellan Skarsgard.’ He didn’t know him and had never worked with him, but had such huge respect.” Trier went to Stockholm and met the star, who then came on board.

Had Haga known the Swedish actor personally before Sentimental Value? “No, I met him during this process,” she noted.

The casting director also shared insight into how Elle Fanning ended up in the film and took her first trip to Oslo. “We worked with an American casting director, Avy Kaufman, and Joachim has an agent in the U.S. who, of course, knows all the big acting agents,” Haga explained why she wasn’t directly involved.

“I was talking to Joachim and saying who I liked, and I was super happy that it ended up being Elle Fanning — for many reasons,” she continued. The facts that she is a bit younger than the sisters and is blonde, while the sisters are dark-haired, already helped. “It’s just a very visually cool contrast,” Haga argued. “And I know that some of the actresses [Trier] was talking to didn’t like the role and didn’t want it because it wasn’t the lead. I personally really like her character, so I thought that was very strange. And Elle Fanning was like nothing like that. She saw the importance of the role and liked the role. Also, she got Oscar-nominated, so she was very grateful and moved.”

Haga also recalled Fanning’s first visit to Oslo to do fittings and rehearsals. “The house that’s in the film is a house in Oslo that they had rented for half a year or so,” she said. “The rehearsals in the film are happening in the house where he’s filming, and we also did the rehearsals in the house, and they asked me to read the other female parts of the scenes. So that was cool for me to be part of a scene with Stellan and Elle, and that was the first time I met her. But it was so meta because we were rehearsing a rehearsal scene and doing it on the location, and she had come over from the U.S., which was her first time in Oslo — like her character. So it was super weird, but very fun.”

#748. What are fossil fuels?

They are in our shampoo bottles, power our cars and heat our homes. But what actually are fossil fuels, and why do they matter?

Whether in the form of crumbly rock, odorless gas or slick black liquid, ancient organic compounds have powered the flourishing of modern life. But now they threaten to make the planet unlivable for many plants, animals and humans.

The collective term refers to coal, oil and natural gas — a group of energy sources that contain carbon and hydrogen.

They started life hundreds of millions of years ago as living plants and animals. When they died, they sank to the bottom of oceans and swamps where they decomposed under layers of sediment.

Over time, this matter was buried deeper and deeper into the earth, subjecting it to increasing pressure and heat which changed its chemical composition. Plants and trees transformed into coal, whereas microscopic plankton and algae became oil and — if the heat and pressure increased further — gas.

Today fossil fuels can be found in the earth's crust all around the world although some countries, such as the US, Saudi Arabia and Russia, have bigger reserves than others.

Coal, found in underground coal beds, is extracted by mining, whereas oil and gas, found in reservoirs beneath the land and ocean, are accessed by drilling.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Since the early 19th Century, when the discovery and exploitation of fossil fuel reserves powered the Industrial Revolution, our use of them has skyrocketed, increasing eight-fold since 1950.

Today they provide 80% of our energy needs through heating, electricity generation and transport.

We transform them into energy either by burning them directly in furnaces that warm up our homes and businesses, or in power plants to heat water into steam which then generates electricity. When it comes to transport, crude oil is refined into a range of products such as diesel, gasoline and kerosene that are burned in the engines of automobiles, airplanes and ships. Natural gas is also sometimes compressed for use in cars and buses.

But fossil fuels are also essential to a huge range of products including steel, formed using a coal-derived material called coke, and plastic, which is produced by refining and processing crude oil and gas.

Fossil fuels are by far the biggest contributors to climate change. When burned to power our modern lives, they emit carbon dioxide (CO2) into Earth's atmosphere, trapping heat and causing temperatures to rise.

With 2025 officially one of the warmest years on record, the impact of these emissions is being felt around the world. Hotter temperatures are causing polar ice caps to melt and creating the conditions for extreme weather events — such as floods, drought, wildfires and storms — to become more intense and frequent.

Scientists stress the need to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to avoid unleashing the most catastrophic impacts of climate change. That was laid out in the 2015 Paris Agreement. Currently, there are 194 parties to the agreement, but progress has been too slow, and overall emissions continue to rise.

Three years after countries agreed at the UN climate conference in Dubai COP28 to transition away from coal, oil and gas. After the previous COP in Brazil failed to reach a consensus on a concrete plan, Brazil has now presented a roadmap aimed at turning that promise into national plans.

"It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable," United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said.

#747. ‘GTA VI’ Industry Domination Will Not End Anytime Soon

Without even having a PC launch date or a 'Grand Theft Auto Online' announcement, Rockstar Games has sold more than 17 million copies of its (latest) masterpiece.

If you’re just waking up from a coma, we’ve got good news. If you’ve been in the coma since 2013, we’ve got really good news.

After 13 years and what has felt like as many delays, Grand Theft Auto VI comes out on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S at midnight (your local time). Finally. Pre-launch, GTA VI is already a smash hit, approaching $1.7 billion in pre-sales (and more than 17 million units sold), according to Sensor Tower data. It is also getting perfect review scores.

Probably no single piece of media has been as highly anticipated as GTA VI, developed and published by Take-Two Interactive imprint Rockstar Games. Some of the excitement is measurable. Last week, GTA VI ranked number one on Screen Engine/ASI’s “Global Attention Share” chart, claiming 5.64 percent of the pie and booting Minecraft out of the spot it held for 45 straight weeks. It was the first time an unreleased game reach first place. Actually, it was the first time an unreleased game ranked better than fourth place (2019’s Call of Duty: Modern Warfare).

GTA VI has now spent 15 weeks in the international research firm’s global top 10, obliterating Modern Warfare‘s record of three weeks. (Screen Engine/ASI balances Google search volume, Twitch and YouTube traffic, and Steam activity to arrive at a proprietary percentage of attention across thousands of games; tracking began in 2019.)

Colan Neese, Screen Engine/ASI’s senior vice president of gaming, tells The Hollywood Reporter he expects GTA VI‘s Global Attention Share will exceed 10 percent when the current week’s numbers come out on Tuesday, Nov. 24. Neese predicts GTA VI will occupy his top spot through at least January 2027.

Gene Park, the digital culture and video games critic for The Washington Post, has already beaten Grand Theft Auto VI. It took him 55 hours of gameplay. (Park and select other reviewers received preview codes — and serious NDAs — from Rockstar.)

But there is so much more for Park in the seemingly endless playground that is Vice City: GTA VI‘s setting based on real-life Miami. Park has since tacked on another 115 hours of gameplay, and is in no way bored.

When we spoke on Wednesday, Park was in the middle of a second full run through the game. This time, he is deliberately making different choices for the protagonists Jason and Lucia. The diverse results, Park says, have been staggering. (Also, he just discovered a zoo after 170 hours of gameplay — that should give you a sense of GTA VI‘s sheer scale.)

There are “just two ways” GTA VI “could have disappointed,” Joost van Dreunen, a video-game industry strategist and NYU professor, told THR. The first would have taken “some kind of awful geopolitical event.” Boy does it feel like we came close during this past week. The second is series of crippling bugs a la Cyberpunk 2077. Rockstar would have never let that happen, van Dreunen said. The publisher would have just delayed GTA VI a third time.

As it is, GTA VI is awesome. After a baker’s-dozen years and an $80-$100 price tag, it had to be. The anticipation (and those delays) has created a “novel… simultaneous synchronized event” experience for a single-player video game, van Dreunen said, which was not possible prior to the digital age. (Rockstar is not releasing GTA VI discs.)

Park believes it will be “a couple of months at the very least” before we get an Online option. GTA V‘s Online component still brings in $300-$500 million per year in revenue, per van Dreunen, through Shark Cash Cards. (You pay real money for in-game currency; Grand Theft Auto Online launched just two weeks after GTA V.)

Van Dreunen says GTA VI will be the dominant video game for “easily” a year, and probably longer. Its coming (but not announced) PC launch and inevitable GTA Online integration (also not announced) will keep the champagne corks popping like, well, Rockstar’s parent company’s stock. Shares of Take-Two Interactive’s Software (TTWO) are up more than 7 percent (from Tuesday’s market close) on those glowing GTA VI reviews — and Wednesday was a down day for the major index funds.

GTA VI officially releases on Thursday. Completely unrelated, boss, I feel a cold coming on…

Jason Nordhaus is at the Center for Computational Relativity and Gravitation and the National Technical Institute for the Deaf, Rochester Institute of Technology, Rochester, New York 14623, USA.

Towards the end of their lives, stars experience a drastic change in their structure as they swell and enter what is known as their giant phase. Because most stars are thought to host orbiting companions (such as planets, other stars or black holes), interesting interactions can happen as the giant host expands. The most striking of these occur when a companion star is engulfed by a giant: astronomers refer to this as the common-envelope phase1. Despite theoretical expectations that common envelopes should be widespread in stellar evolution, they have been extraordinarily difficult to observe. Writing in Nature, however, Karambelkar et al.2 report the first direct detection of a star inside a giant star.

#744. Jensen Huang: Spy row, affairs leave Nvidia without its rockstar CEO

Jensen Huang, who built Nvidia into the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, is stepping down as CEO over extramarital affairs. DW examines how losing its figurehead will affect the firm and the US-China AI race.

Nvidia's board met late Wednesday to decide on CEO Jensen Huang's future as reports emerged of other extramarital affairs — this time with employees.

In a statement issued on Thursday, the world's most valuable chip supplier said Huang was resigning as President, CEO and board member, effective immediately.

The firm added that current Vice President and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress would become interim CEO.

Under Nvidia's bylaws, Huang can be removed "with or without cause" by a majority vote of its 11 directors.

The New York Times first reported that the 63-year-old Huang had an affair with a senior Nvidia executive who reported directly to him.

Later Thursday, Reuters news agency alleged an intimate relationship between Huang and a second employee, citing unidentified sources.

Those revelations emerged just three days after Huang admitted a relationship with a Chinese woman, whom United States intelligence agencies believe was spying for China. The woman, Alice Huang — no relation — is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm that runs artificial intelligence (AI) data centers across Southeast Asia and is a major client of Nvidia.

The US government is investigating the startup on suspicion that it secretly sent some of its Nvidia chips to China, violating Washington's curbs on high-end semiconductors.

Those advanced Nvidia processors ‌are ​used to train and run the large AI models behind chatbots and other generative AI products.

Megaspeed denies the allegations and on Thursday pledged to cooperate with US investigators.  Huang, the alleged spy, has been barred from entering Singapore and Taiwan — a key chipmaking island.

While Nvidia's board backed its CEO after the first scandal emerged, market watchers believe the second caused too much reputational damage to one of the world's top three companies by market value.

According to The Wall Street Journal, Huang doesn't believe in formal succession planning, so with little notice, Nvidia appointed CFO Kress as interim CEO.

Bloomberg reported Wednesday that Nvidia’s board is working with advisers to identify potential permanent successors.

Kress, other senior Nvidia executives and members of Huang's own family have been mooted as replacements. The family members include his daughter Madison, a senior director of product marketing, and his son Spencer, who currently works in the firm's robotics division.

Rumors also abound over a longer-term solution. On India's CNBC-TV18, Jeffrey Sonnenfeld from the Yale School of Management floated former Apple CEO Tim Cook and ex-Google CEO Eric Schmidt.

US President Donald Trump also backed Cook on social media, writing: "A Legend replaces a Legend."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The scandals have certainly hit Nvidia's market value. Since the first extramarital affair emerged on Sunday, the chipmaker's market capitalization has fallen by well over $600 billion to $4.2 trillion.

Nvidia shares were down more than 9% in premarket trading Thursday, after dropping by 10% earlier this week. Some analysts expect the stock price to struggle in the short term.

Nvidia stock hit all-time highs just a month ago as US technology giants continued to announce billions in spending on AI infrastructure.

Demand for Nvidia's advanced chips is so high, however, that many market analysts expect little impact on near-term sales.

"While Jensen [Huang] is the heart and lungs of the Nvidia story…the company and its leading-edge GPU technology will go on and [his departure] does not change the entrenched position Nvidia has in the AI Revolution chip arms race," said Dan Ives, a partner, senior managing director and tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, a US-based merchant bank

Analysts see the biggest long-term risk in strategy and execution. After all, Huang was the leader who picked which ideas Nvidia should bet heavily on and got the whole company behind them.

His sudden exit is also seen as highly disruptive to the chip designer's strong relationships with AI hyperscalers, Taiwanese chip producer TSMC and foreign governments — especially China.

Huang was Nvidia's main lobbyist on US chip export rules and persuaded US President Donald Trump to ease some curbs on China last year.

Huang is often called a rockstar CEO for his leather jackets instead of suits.

Like Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, he was also seen as a key-person risk as Nvidia’s public image, strategic direction and technical decisions became closely tied to him.

Huang steered the company for more than three decades and was also respected for his hands-on involvement in product architecture and engineering decisions.

He also insisted on a flat management structure, with around 60 executives reporting directly to him.

Huang has run the company so tightly around his own technical judgment and product decisions that investors may have little sense of how it would function without him.

At the same time, Nvidia is no longer the startup Huang founded in 1993. The company has built deep expertise in chip design and software, creating a durable moat that helps protect its huge profits, which topped $120.1 billion last year.

Some analysts argue that its central role in the AI hardware buildout makes it less dependent on Huang’s day-to-day input.

China is quickly playing catch-up with the US in the global race for AI dominance.

While Chinese AI models have lagged behind the likes of ChatGPT and Claude, recent updates from DeepSeek, Alibaba and Moonshot have closed much of the gap on benchmark tests and often beat US rivals on cost and speed.

Beijing is also investing heavily in domestic chips and data centers to reduce reliance on US hardware.

The US has curbed exports to China of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips.

However, this move has only slowed the pace of China's AI ambitions.

Reuters reported Thursday that Chinese AI firms are now trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centers outside China, amid fears the US could further tighten restrictions on advanced chips.

Also Thursday, Beijing accused the US of using the Nvidia spying claims as a pretext to impose a technological "blockade" on China.

The issue is likely to dominate talks next week between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC gathering in Shenzhen in southern China.

This year’s CMAs will air on Wednesday, Nov. 18 at 8 p.m. PT/ET on ABC, available to stream live via DirecTV (with a five-day free trial), YouTube TV (with a 10-day free trial), Fubo (with a five-day free trial), Sling and Hulu + Live TV.

#742. Rose Byrne on What Lured Her to ‘The Good Daughter’ and Why That Complicated Ending Wraps the Series

The star and executive producer unpacks the thrilling Peacock mystery also starring Meghann Fahy and if what happens to the young girl at the center of it is fair.

[This story contains major spoilers from The Good Daughter finale.]

Rose Byrne keeps outdoing herself. Her explosive limited series The Good Daughter co-starring Meghann Fahy quickly became the top show on Peacock. Just last year, she grabbed a best actress Oscar nomination and won both the Golden Globe and Independent Spirits Award for If I Had Legs I’d Kick You — the film nobody saw coming. She also wrapped season two of her Apple TV comedy Platonic.

Even for an actress with a pedigree like Byrne’s spanning over 30 years, projects like The Good Daughter are rare opportunities, she shared last year while still filming in the Atlanta Metro area. “Sam is the sort of role written for a man,” the Australian actress confessed. “It’s very dominant, kind of self-possessed, and she has physical trauma. Like she has scars, and she has a history. She has all this rich stuff that’s not always the case with the female roles you read.” Related Stories Beyond the Book Karin Slaughter Said "Absolutely Not" to Adapting Her Novel 'The Good Daughter.' Then She Wrote the Whole Series TV 'The Good Daughter' Review: Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy Elevate Peacock's Overly Familiar Southern-Fried Thriller

It’s the kind of story that Byrne, who also serves as executive producer alongside fellow Aussie, Big Little Lies Emmy winner Bruna Papandrea, sees as bestselling author and fellow EP Karin Slaughter’s superpower. “She writes incredibly rich female characters who are complicated and complex, and not all good and not all bad, and who have a lot to work with,” Byrne continued.

For the first time ever, Slaughter, who has had other books grace the screen with Pieces of Her for Netflix and, of course, Will Trent for ABC, adapted her own work and served as showrunner. The psychological thriller revolves around estranged sisters Samantha and Charlotte Quinn who, as teens, suffer a brutal attack in response to their father Rusty’s (an excellent Brendan Gleeson) work as an attorney that has left them scarred. Partial blindness and a permanent limp serve as enduring physical reminders for Sam. Spared many of the physical scars, Charlie’s show up in other ways. And they both lost their beloved mother Gamma (an effective Olivia Williams).

As the older sister, Sam sacrificed herself to ensure Charlie would be hurt the least, but that act created emotional and physical distance between the two. Rusty’s failing health has brought Sam back home from New York City, where she is a patent lawyer, to Pikeville, Georgia. It’s his defense of Kelly Wilson (impressive newcomer Shayna Benardo), a special needs high school girl seemingly behind a horrific school shooting that killed the school’s principal and a freshman girl that keeps her there.

What seems like an open-and-shut case is anything but. Because Charlie witnessed part of the shooting and is also an attorney, the two women can’t avoid each other. Any degree of separation disappears in a small town, especially for a polarizing case like this one, so emotional landmines abound. As the mystery surrounding Kelly’s actions lingers, the attack that the sisters survived years before also figures more prominently, forcing both Sam and Charlie to tackle all they have left unsaid and unresolved.

“One of the pleasures of this is that I wrote everything from the perspective of two women. So much to probably Meghann and Rose’s dismay, one of them always has to be in every single scene, because we get their perspective, and it’s a very internalized kind of storytelling,” Slaughter said on set. “But also, in a way, it shows their growth as sisters and as daughters, and gives me an opportunity to frame something that happens every day in America, basically through these very personal stories of these sisters who have been victims of violence before.”

On set when speaking to The Hollywood Reporter, Byrne noted “it’s rare you get to work side by side with a fellow actress.” That female energy is also directly sustained behind the camera with Oscar and Emmy-nominated director Steph Green (New Boy, Duster, Watchmen) and Australian cinematographer Zoë White (The Handmaid’s Tale). Below, she probes beyond the many plot twists to delve into aspects of the series that move her professionally and emotionally. Of course, we asked if there would be more and if she felt what happens to Kelly, the young girl at the center of the mystery, is fair.

In addition to playing Sam, you’re also an executive producer. What made you want to take on roles in front and behind the camera?

Being an EP was really like more of a seat at the table, particularly with casting. Getting Meghann Fahy on board was a huge deal for us. She’s so effervescent as Charlie; so magnetic and funny and heartbreaking. You just believe her straight away. She jumps. She lights up the screen, and she’s just gorgeous. I adore her. She’s so extraordinary, so talented.

And then Brendan Gleeson, who’s a legend at this point — so extraordinary and such a gifted storyteller — and so magnanimous with his work. I’ve known him since I was 23 when I did Troy. So that was a great thread. I worked with his son Domhnall Gleeson, so it was a lovely full circle to then have him playing my father. And that’s a tough character; it’s very polarizing. There’s a lot of fury that my character has at her father, a lot of anger and disappointment, and Brendan makes that hard because he’s so charming, but that’s what makes it interesting.

Reading the screenplay and the novel… it’s a classic origin story for Sam, where going back to where she came from, she’s dealing with all of her truths and all of the lies, and trying to uncover the past through this case; understanding her father more, but it felt to me almost a role written for a man, not particularly something you would see necessarily for a female character. That really intrigued me.

How did you pull off Sam’s physical transformation to convey her disability or disabilities?

Well, she has dysarthria, [her] speech disability from her trauma, and so I worked with my voice coach Kate Wilson, who’s extraordinary. She’s the head of voice [and speech] at Juilliard. I’ve worked with her for years and she’s incredible. She’s the most alive, passionate, compassionate teacher, and she’s really very sage. She and I delved in with what that would sound like, listening to tapes and recordings, and also working on the accent of Georgia and how my character had lived in New York for 20 years, and what it would sound like returning, and when it would return, and in what situations. When I return to Australia, my accent becomes a lot broader, and you know how you’re influenced by your environment.

Then with the limp, I worked with this wonderful PT trainer who works in rehab with people who’ve suffered injuries and so on. We homed in on what her limp would look like, and then did a million videos and would send them to Steph and figure out how far to go with it because we didn’t want it ever to be comical. Sometimes what reads on screen is very different in real life.

The younger Charlie [Drew Ann Cheek] and Sam [Audrey Grace Marshall] really match the older Charlie and Sam.

I was very front seat with the casting of that, so there was a lot of weighing in with everybody about who we felt the best lead was and, also, physically you have to have a lot of resemblance to them. I thought the girls were so wonderful, and that’s again a very hard job to do. I thought they just captured both Meghann and myself in really specific ways, and we watched a lot of footage of them as well. With Sam, obviously there’s a real before and after physically with what she goes through, so that was something I had to separately have work on. But establishing them as young women was so important.

While Sam and Charlie, in particular, experience extraordinary circumstances, the series seems to center on this whole idea of women holding onto very traumatic events or violations but still functioning in their lives.

Which we do every day. If you read the statistics about it, like one in six women have been sexually assaulted. A lot of people in America have suffered gun violence in their families. These statistics are horrific, and we worked very closely with RAINN who work with survivors of rape and incest and other horrific things, and they were incredible. We always had resources on set if people were being triggered or needed to talk. It was a safe space.

To Steph Green, our director, my first question was: “How will this be portrayed? I’m not interested in anything gratuitous or exploitative.” And Steph was so determined to tell the story in a way that had none of those tonal qualities in it. So absolutely the story has elements of trauma, but it’s dealt with in a very delicate way that I think is powerful but never gratuitous or exploitative.

Speaking of Steph, the way she, and Zoë White the cinematographer, handle the traumatic flashbacks is such an innovative technique that I don’t think I’ve seen.

I agree. I remember her telling me about that, how she was going to focus on hands and this and moments and shoot close-ups of various things to sort of link the story. And it’s beautifully told. The sense of memory was really vivid, I felt, [in] a lot of those flashbacks to me. I feel like they achieved something quite innovative.

When Rusty dies, everything is understandably sad. But the coffin scene at the funeral home manages to be both light and heavy. Did it come at a time when you guys kind of needed a break?

Meghann was so heartbreaking in that scene, and she’s so funny, too. That was actually great because what was harder was the flashback scene when we’re in New York, and it precipitates the estrangement. That scene was a lot harder because we’re through a closed door, sort of screaming a monologue and it’s a flashback, and I’ve got a wig on. That to me was more of a leap of faith. I think that was a harder needle to thread. Whereas the coffin scene, as you called it, was so gratifying to be able to look at her and really have a scene like two actors opposite one another and have such rich material. It was definitely strange for Brendan because he was in the coffin for a little bit. That’s no fun. But that was a scene I was both scared and excited to do.

There are so many powerful scenes, what are some of your favorite moments, or what stands out most to you?

The scene that haunts me so much is when Charlie confronts Judith over the kitchen table. I remember reading it in the novel, and I remember the first one I read in the screenplay, and my hair on my body was just standing on end. It was so suspenseful, so tightly drawn, and the history alone between these two women across each other from this table to then reach this boiling point of this scene was just masterful storytelling.

And it’s interesting because Sam and Charlie don’t have that traumatic relationship with them that Kelly has. Then considering that she’s special needs. So it’s unfathomable that the Pinkmans could do something like this to Kelly, right?

Yeah Karin, she’s a master storyteller, and just when you think you know where something is going. I found myself reading the novel and reading the screenplay [drawn to] the turns of what these people do and the perspectives that she puts on each situation. But that scene still haunts me.

I think it’s a very, very complicated answer and question. It’s such a nuanced and complicated story that has led her to this horrific situation that we made her in at the beginning. I really was fascinated with the process of that. I spoke to many lawyers who work in the criminal justice system about the process and how it works, and where you end up, and how you interrogate a witness, and like the defense team, and all of that. And Karin so beautifully captures how hard that system is and how it fails again and again and again for people, but how also you can have some wins. But it’s very nuanced and it’s very complicated.

It was a learning curve for me to even begin to understand that. So I think [Karin] has such a great understanding of that, and also the genre of a thriller, you know, and creating the suspense of that. Right until the very last episode, you’re really on the edge of your seat, as she just twists and turns and uses the perspective of one character then the other, and you constantly have shifting alliances, and she’s just very unflinching in her portrait of things. And that’s brave.

That’s why I ask if what happens to Kelly is fair because it’s very clear in the end how manipulated she was. And given her mental capacity, she wasn’t really aware of what she was doing.

Do you see a continuation to The Good Daughter?

I don’t. It feels contained to this series, like the novel, to me. I have hope for the characters that they would, I mean, selfishly, continue to have a better relationship with one another after all the trauma and all the things they’ve weathered or the storms they’ve weathered. But it felt, to me, pretty contained about this specific thing they had to go through.

I’m sure you take lessons from each project that you do. What is your biggest takeaway from this one?

I think diving back into this genre was really interesting for me [because] I hadn’t done it for many years. [There are] tropes that are really fun in there, and the challenges of a very complicated plot at times, and being ahead of it for myself. But Karin, the author, is really ahead of everybody. So, it was interesting. Also to work with an author who then wrote the screenplay, that was also something I’d never done creatively, and how fun that was. Also, we would have rigorous conversations where we would disagree about things, and that was fun too. I think I learned a lot.

All six episodes of The Good Daughter are streaming on Peacock.
